concepts.decision: Find the dominant trust boundary and credible consequence before choosing a mitigation.
concepts.definition: Weakness arising from a system’s components, boundaries, dependencies, or operating pattern.
concepts.failureExample: A design scans components but ignores the shared admin path connecting them.
concepts.label: Architecture Vulnerability

concepts.decision: Map data, identity, configuration, logs, recovery, and contracts to owners.
concepts.definition: Allocation of cloud security tasks across provider and customer layers.
concepts.failureExample: A cloud account is exposed because the provider service existed but customer IAM was broad.
concepts.label: Cloud Shared Responsibility

concepts.decision: Assess each service identity, call, data flow, and authorization point.
concepts.definition: Small independently deployed services that communicate over multiple interfaces.
concepts.failureExample: An internal service trusts any caller on the cluster network.
concepts.label: Microservices

concepts.decision: Assess image source, registry, runtime, host, secrets, and orchestrator controls.
concepts.definition: Packaging workloads with dependencies into deployable images and runtimes.
concepts.failureExample: A privileged container image from an untrusted registry reaches production.
concepts.label: Containerization

concepts.decision: Assess event source, function identity, permissions, package, retries, and observability.
concepts.definition: Provider-managed execution triggered by events or requests without customer server management.
concepts.failureExample: An internal event invokes a function that performs an unapproved financial action.
concepts.label: Serverless

concepts.decision: Assess firmware support, physical access, interfaces, update path, and consequence.
concepts.definition: Network-connected devices that sense, act, or collect data in constrained environments.
concepts.failureExample: A field sensor retains a default credential and cannot receive a safe update.
concepts.label: Iot

concepts.decision: Prioritize safety, process consequence, segmentation, and approved change methods.
concepts.definition: System that monitors or controls physical industrial processes.
concepts.failureExample: An aggressive scan disrupts a controller that drives a physical process.
concepts.label: Industrial Control System

concepts.decision: Assess intermittent links, remote physical exposure, local data, and remote recovery.
concepts.definition: Processing near data sources rather than only in a central environment.
concepts.failureExample: A remote edge node stores sensitive data after losing central connectivity.
concepts.label: Edge Computing

concepts.decision: Treat host, management API, templates, and virtual networking as high-impact paths.
concepts.definition: Shared-hardware workload isolation through a hypervisor and virtual infrastructure.
concepts.failureExample: A compromised hypervisor crosses expected guest boundaries.
concepts.label: Virtualization

concepts.decision: Assess authorization, interfaces, backups, replication, logs, and administrator separation.
concepts.definition: Protection of persistent, high-value data and the paths that administer or query it.
concepts.failureExample: A service account bypasses intended application checks on sensitive tables.
concepts.label: Database Security

concepts.decision: Enforce object and action authorization at the server for every request.
concepts.definition: Protection of programmatic interfaces through authenticated, authorized, validated requests.
concepts.failureExample: A user changes an identifier and retrieves another customer’s record.
concepts.label: API Security

concepts.decision: Assess provenance, update authority, dependency integrity, and recovery.
concepts.definition: Risk introduced through suppliers, dependencies, build paths, updates, or support logistics.
concepts.failureExample: A trusted update channel distributes a compromised package.
concepts.label: Supply Chain Risk

misconceptions.correction: The provider operates infrastructure, while the customer still owns identities, code, data, configuration, event sources, and monitoring.

outcome: Identify the dominant architectural trust boundary or failure path in a modern system and recommend a proportionate mitigation direction.

sections.body: Cloud and serverless designs move responsibilities across provider and customer boundaries. Microservices and APIs multiply service identities, interfaces, and policy points. Containers and virtualization add images, orchestration, runtime, and management planes. IoT, embedded, edge, and industrial systems add physical exposure, constrained patching, safety, legacy protocols, and remote-support dependencies. Databases remain sensitive concentration points for data and privilege.
keyPoints: Assess each layer and interface, not only the application code.
Availability and safety consequences can dominate in industrial and edge contexts.
sections.title: Architecture changes the attack and failure surface

sections.body: Segment trust zones, minimize identities and privileges, authenticate and authorize APIs, protect secrets, verify images and updates, harden management planes, log critical actions, plan safe patching, and test recovery. In a distributed design, also address consistency, latency, dependency failure, and observability. A mitigation is credible only if it suits the architecture’s operational constraints and has an owner.
keyPoints: Management and orchestration paths often have greater blast radius than one workload.
Shared responsibility must be converted into named control ownership.

summary: Client, server, database, cloud, distributed, IoT, container, serverless, embedded, edge, and industrial systems expose different trust boundaries, management planes, update paths, and failure modes. Assess the architecture rather than applying one generic checklist.

assumptions: Only entities and claims anchored in the canonical unit or explicitly labeled hypothetical scenario are used.
A highlighted path means the learner is inspecting that path; it does not assert the event occurred.
The current source is authoritative for facts; this treatment reorganizes presentation without changing canonical content.
The lesson teaches one bounded decision and does not claim to exhaust every jurisdiction, vendor implementation, architecture, attack, or exception.
teaching.focalRelation: Architecture labels do not identify the decisive path; client, API, service, container, orchestrator, database, cloud control plane, edge/IoT/industrial device, update supplier, and operator create different trust changes.

learningJob.plainExplanation: Architecture labels do not identify the decisive failure path. The analyst must locate the actual identity, update authority, boundary, management path, consequence, and evidence for the selected system.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: Coordinated architecture comparisons should make those dimensions stable across families; the current single edge-to-cloud map adds only one example and cannot teach the advertised breadth.
